newsitem.title: BELGIUM: GEC official pessimistic on defence restructuring.
newsitem.headline: GEC official pessimistic on defence restructuring.

text.p: A senior official of British defence engineering giant General Electric Co Plc warned on Tuesday that the European defence industry could be "wiped out" if Europe failed to meet the structural challenges ahead.
Sir Geoffrey Pattie, chairman of GEC defence division GEC-Marconi, also said he was pessimistic about the industry undertaking the necessary restructuring in time.

"I don't believe that the European defence industry will come together in time before it's engulfed by the United States," he told a press conference. This would not be so much in western Europe. "It is the third market where we will be competing with the Americans."
Pattie took part in a conference in Brussels on Europe's defence industry. The need for industry consolidation was a dominant theme among speakers.

"The problem of course is that we can't go out and merge like the United States companies are doing so spectacularly because of the regulatory framework and the fact that we are all working for different countries," Pattie said.

However, saying there was a "remaining faint hope", Pattie said governments must accept the nature of the threat and then say they are prepared to subordinate some of their other aims to achieve what many people agree needs to be done.

He mentioned the case of Thomson-CSF, the French defence firm which the previous conservative government had planned to privatise. This is now uncertain following the Socialist election victory this month.

GEC had put in a bid for Thomson after being encouraged to do so by "one part" of the French government. But, he added, "another part of the French government then said: 'No, we'd rather you didn't, kindly go away'."
Pattie said there were other such examples and that he was not launching "some anti-French government thing".
But he stressed that governments must allow the creation of firms which could become "world class", saying there were "hardly any, if any", such European aerospace firms now.
They must then be prepared to handle "second order" problems, for example involving closures of factories.

He asked whether governments were prepared to promote world class competitiveness, in which case they would allow the regulatory regime to soften and allow the mergers to take place. And would they then be prepared to "stomach and accept the consequences" in terms of reduced employment?
"...unless we can actually structurally meet this challenge we'll be wiped out altogether," Pattie warned.
